newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat media rejects US criticism on Serb refugees.
newsitem.headline: Croat media rejects US criticism on Serb refugees.

text.p: Croatian media on Tuesday rejected U.S. criticism minority Serbs were being prevented from returning to their homes, saying most who fled in 1995 had no wish to come back.

John Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European Affairs, on Monday accused Zagreb of intimidating Serbs trying to come home under the 1995 Dayton peace accord that ended years of war in former Yugoslavia.
Official Croatian media rejected the U.S. criticism, saying 13,000 Serbs had returned but most of the rest -- at least 150,000 -- had no desire to live in an independent Croatia.

Minority Serbs seized almost a third of Croatia in a 1991 uprising against its secession from federal Yugoslavia, driving out 250,000 Croats. They lost all but the Eastern Slavonia enclave to Croatian counter-offensives in 1995.
State television said in a commentary Serbs chose to heed the orders of their rebel leadership to flee Croatia before the arrival of Croatian troops reconquering the separatist region.
The flagship state-run newspaper Vjesnik said foreign critics ignored the plight of tens of thousands of Croat war refugees who had not seen their homes for up to five years.
Around 80,000 Croat refugees are waiting to return to Eastern Slavonia, the last separatist Serb enclave, pending its transfer back to government rule next year by a transitional U.N. administration.
"The prime task of Croatia is certainly not the return of Serbs. The war was waged on Croatian soil, not in Serbia. It was Serbs who hounded Croats out of their homes," said Vjesnik.

"The prime objective of Croatia is to stand on its own borders and resume control over its whole territory. Everything else follows from that in a natural sequence, including a carefully controlled return of Serbs who wish to do so."
Kornblum said Croatia's nationalist authorities had "failed to protect (Serb) victims (from intimidation) and often perpetrated the crimes.
"These heinous acts send a chilling message to those who remain in Eastern Slavonia and those who might return to other parts of Croatia," he told a U.N. conference in Geneva.
